scenes.visual: Title card: Cells Hold Their Size.

scenes.tts: Cells do not just end up a size. Growing cells hold their size by linking growth to division. A fission yeast cell divides only once it reaches a set size. Born small, it grows more first. Born large, it grows less. That matters, because size sets how much a cell can make and how much room each part gets. The nucleus, for one, grows with the cell. So how does a cell know its size?
scenes.visual: Two rod-shaped fission yeast cells, one born short and one born long, grow at their ends to the same length and then divide in the middle; a nucleus in each grows with the cell.

So how does a cell know its size?

scenes.tts: One way is dilution. In budding yeast, every newborn cell gets about the same amount of a brake on division, a protein called W H I five. As the cell grows, the brake is diluted. A big cell dilutes it sooner and is more likely to commit to dividing. A cell born small waits, and grows more first.
scenes.visual: A small and a large newborn yeast cell each hold the same number of red brake dots; as each grows the dots spread out, and a 'commit' light turns on first in the larger cell.
scenes.narration: One way is dilution. In budding yeast, every newborn cell gets about the same amount of a brake on division, a protein called Whi5. As the cell grows, the brake is diluted. scenes.tts: Size also sets what a cell can make. To keep its molecules at the same concentration, a growing cell must make more R N A and protein. Most cells do, roughly in step with volume. That has a limit. Budding yeast held so they grow without dividing get many times bigger, and synthesis falls behind. Their cytoplasm becomes diluted.
scenes.visual: A growing cell keeps the same density of RNA and protein dots; then an arrested cell balloons and its dots thin out, labelled 'diluted'.

scenes.tts: The parts scale too, but their shares depend on the cell. A little more than a quarter of one hamster cell line is nucleus. In fission yeast it is under one tenth. There, the nucleus grows with the cell across a thirty-five-fold range of sizes, and a sixteen-fold change in D N A leaves the ratio unchanged.
scenes.visual: Two stacked bars: V79 hamster cell with the nucleus share near a quarter, fission yeast with the nucleus share under a tenth; then a row of fission yeast cells of rising size, each nucleus growing in proportion.

scenes.tts: Plant cells take a short cut. In Arabidopsis root epidermis, cells grew about fourteen-fold in volume, but the space between vacuole and cell boundary grew only about two to threefold. Most new volume is vacuole, and the wall has to loosen to let the cell stretch.
scenes.visual: A root epidermal cell elongates; its vacuole swells to fill most of it while the cytoplasm layer stays thin; the wall is drawn stretching.

scenes.tts: Geometry adds a cost to being big. Everything a cell takes in crosses its surface. Everything it uses is spread through its volume. Double a sphere's radius, and its area rises fourfold while its volume rises eightfold. With fixed uptake per area and fixed demand per volume, supply falls behind past some radius.
scenes.visual: A sphere grows from 5 to 10 micrometres; area bar grows 4 times, volume bar 8 times; supply and demand curves cross.

scenes.tts: Keep the order. Cells set their size by linking growth to division. Size then sets what they can make and how their parts share the room. Surface and volume add a cost, not a universal maximum.
